L42@P6: Abstract
L43@P6: Fire in buildings can have a severe impact in terms of both human safety and
L44@P6: potential economic loss. This is especially true in the case of fires of such severity
L45@P6: that the building structure is damaged.
L46@P6: Concrete buildings are traditionally regarded as safe in a fire situation as concrete is
L47@P6: non-flammable and exhibits highly insulating material properties. The majority of
L48@P6: current research relating to the impact of fire on structures examines other forms of
L49@P6: construction. Research of concrete in fire is generally limited to investigation and
L50@P6: testing of individual members in order to understand the often complex interactions
L51@P6: exhibited by concrete as a material at high temperatures.
L52@P6: This research seeks to redress the balance by using a systematic approach to examine
L53@P6: effects of fire on a holistic concrete structure in simplified but realistic temperature
L54@P6: exposures. The research utilises evidence and structural information from the
L55@P6: Windsor Tower in Madrid, which suffered a major fire in February 2005 with partial
L56@P6: collapse in some areas of the structure. The fire spread throughout the building,
L57@P6: travelling both upwards and downwards.
L58@P6: Computer modelling was used extensively. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD)
L59@P6: analysis was used to explore likely fire temperature and duration in localised areas.
L60@P6: Structural Finite Element Modelling (FEM) was used to develop a hierarchy of
L61@P6: models, beginning with simple structural forms and progressing logically to more
L62@P6: detailed structures. This produced a systematic and comprehensive analysis of the
L63@P6: reaction of the structure to fire for comparison to the real, observable damage to the
L64@P6: building and assessment of generic failure behaviours.
L65@P6: The structural model produced was used with a number of variations in support
L66@P6: condition, fire spread rate and extent, and fire protection. It was found that for a
L67@P6: structure of this type, structural stiffness of the concrete floors was insufficient to
L68@P6: compensate for the loss of strength in heated steel members where there was no
L69@P6-7: alternative load redistribution path. Tall Concrete Buildings Subjected to Vertically Moving Fires:
